paragraphs.heading: Gravity as the shape of spacetime
paragraphs.text: General relativity is Albert Einstein's theory of gravity, published in May 1916. It is the description of gravity for large objects that modern physics accepts today. It describes gravity as a geometric property of space and time taken together, which is called four-dimensional spacetime. The theory generalizes special relativity, and it also refines Isaac Newton's law of gravitation.

paragraphs.heading: Matter bends spacetime
paragraphs.text: The core idea is that the curvature of spacetime is tied to the energy, momentum and stress of whatever is there, including matter and radiation. That link is written down in the Einstein field equations, a set of second-order partial differential equations. The physicist John Archibald Wheeler put it in one line: spacetime tells matter how to move, and matter tells spacetime how to curve. These equations are nonlinear and are thought to be hard to solve. Einstein used approximations to work out the theory's initial predictions.

paragraphs.heading: Where Newton still works
paragraphs.text: Newton's law of gravity is not thrown away. It can be seen as what general relativity predicts when spacetime is almost flat and the masses involved are not moving. Beyond that, the new theory makes predictions Newton's law cannot. They concern how time passes, the geometry of space, how bodies fall freely and how light travels, and among them are gravitational lensing, gravitational time dilation, the Shapiro time delay, the gravitational redshift of light, black holes and singularities.

paragraphs.heading: An eight-year search
paragraphs.text: In 1907 Einstein began with a simple thought experiment about an observer in free fall and set out to find a relativistic theory of gravity. The search took eight years, with many detours and false starts. A kind of non-Euclidean geometry called Riemannian geometry gave him the mathematical frame he needed, an idea pointed out by the mathematician Marcel Grossmann and published by the two men in 1913. In November 1915 Einstein presented the field equations to the Prussian Academy of Science.

paragraphs.heading: The first tests
paragraphs.text: In 1915 Einstein showed that his theory accounted for the puzzling perihelion advance of the planet Mercury without any arbitrary adjustable numbers. In 1919 an expedition led by Eddington checked the predicted deflection of starlight by the Sun during a total solar eclipse on 29 May. The result agreed with the theory and made Einstein famous overnight. So far, every test of general relativity has agreed with it.

paragraphs.heading: Black holes, lenses and waves
paragraphs.text: The theory predicts black holes, regions where space and time are so distorted that nothing, not even light, can get out. In 1916 Karl Schwarzschild found the first exact non-trivial solution of the field equations, which later underpinned the modern picture of black holes. The theory also predicts gravitational lensing, where bent light produces distorted or repeated images of one distant object. It predicts gravitational waves too, and these have been observed directly by LIGO and other observatories.

paragraphs.heading: The universe as a whole
paragraphs.text: In 1917 Einstein applied the theory to the entire universe, starting relativistic cosmology. He assumed the universe was static and added a cosmological constant to his equations to allow for that, but by 1929 Hubble and others had shown the universe is expanding. Lemaître used expanding solutions found by Friedmann in 1922 to build the earliest Big Bang models. Einstein later called the cosmological constant the biggest blunder of his life.

paragraphs.heading: What is still unsolved
paragraphs.text: Despite rival theories, general relativity remains the simplest one that fits the experimental data. Its open problem is quantum physics: nobody has found a self-consistent theory of quantum gravity. Nor is it known yet how to unify gravity with the other three interactions, the strong, weak and electromagnetic forces.
